children: By Dewi Kurniawati

Indonesia's arabica coffee output is taking a hit from last year's devastating floods, with farmers in Aceh province reporting lower yields from the early harvest which is set to gather pace next month, farmers and analysts said.
Floods and landslides killed more than 1,000 people in late 2025, washing away trees and damaging 17,070 hectares (42,181 acres) of coffee estates.

Expectations for lower coffee output in Indonesia, the world's fourth-largest producer, come as ICE arabica futures hit a five-week low on Thursday thanks to favourable weather and upbeat prospects for global supply.

"The decline is already visible," said Rizwan, a coffee farmer who heads a cooperative representing 6,000 growers in Central Aceh, adding that small volumes were already being picked ahead of the main harvest in October.
This is the region's first coffee harvest after the flooding and landslide damage.
Production on the worst-affected farms could decline by 30% to 40% from a year earlier, Rizwan said by phone from his home in Takengon.
Some plantations remained buried and others were swept away, with surviving trees bearing less fruit because floodwaters stripped away the humus-rich topsoil.
Aceh, home to the renowned Gayo arabica variety, accounts for nearly 10% of Indonesia's coffee production and about a quarter of its arabica output.

While output is expected to rise in Brazil, Vietnam, Ethiopia and parts of Central America, Indonesia's crop is forecast to fall by 1 million bags to 11.38 million 60-kilogram bags in 2026/27, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Indonesia accounts for approximately 6% of global coffee output.

Production in flood-affected areas could fall by around 25%, said Daryl Kryst, senior vice president for soft and agricultural commodities in Asia at StoneX, a financial services firm. Some exporters have said they expect losses as high as 35%.
Aceh exports as much as 90% of its higher-grade beans.

"The impact is likely to be concentrated in the specialty coffee export market and should become more visible in the next annual production cycle, as major weather events often take one or two harvests to fully affect output," Kryst said.
The October 2027 harvest could be more severely affected, he added.
Indonesia's government has approved additional post-disaster funding to rehabilitate 12,739 hectares (31,479 acres) through replanting, expansion and yield-improvement programmes.
However, replacing damaged trees will constrain exports for several seasons, as newly planted arabica trees typically take three to four years to produce commercially viable harvests, Kryst said.
Rizwan said the coffee seedlings distributed by the government were too small for planting and were not expected to be in the ground until the end of 2026.
Meanwhile, a looming dry spell due to a strong El Niño could trigger insufficient moisture, premature flower loss, poor fruit formation and lower bean quality.
